name: Uma Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Uma. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Of course. I'm Uma, 27, and I'm an apprentice lineworker with the electricity company, nearly two years in. I'm married to Yusuf, who works in his father's hardware shop on Station Road, and we live in the flat above it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Then let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Our crew looks after the hill country west of town, so lots of long single lines on wooden poles running to farms. Day to day it's maintenance: replacing insulators, cutting back trees, fixing damage after wind. On a storm night, the farmers up the valley don't care if you're a man or a woman. They care that the milking machines start at five. I'm the only woman on the crew, and my foreman Gareth treats me like everyone else, which is all I ask.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into the trade?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My uncle Karim was a lineman for 30 years. He told me an apprenticeship was worth more than a degree I'd be paying off forever, and he was right. I use an AI chatbot now and then to check my exam answers, but mostly I learn by watching Gareth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. Steady is good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what my uncle said all along: real work still needs real people. I'd say it after Friday prayers and to the crew. I don't really post things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much changes, and that suits me. My job is outdoors and hands-on. My uncle Karim got me into this trade when everyone said a girl shouldn't climb poles. In this picture I get to prove everyone wrong slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship and keep putting 200 a month aside. Yusuf and I want to buy a small house within three years, so that's where the money goes. I'd keep using the chatbot for exam practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything on your mind already, money or family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The shop, a little. Yusuf's dad is getting older, and the big online stores keep cutting prices. We've got about four months saved, so we're fine, but we keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of the routine tasks in your day might AI take, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fault reports, maybe. Right now Gareth phones them in at the end of the day. A computer could write them up from our photos, and he'd be glad.

say: Real work still needs **real people**, as my uncle always said.
I'd say it after **Friday prayers** and to the crew, not online.
think: My **hands-on** outdoor job barely changes, which suits me.
I'd get to prove the **doubters** wrong, slowly, the way my uncle Karim did.
do: Finish the **apprenticeship** and keep learning from Gareth.
Save **200 a month** toward a house with Yusuf within three years.
feel: **Calm** and content with a steady path.
S0.quote: My uncle Karim got me into this trade when everyone said a girl shouldn't climb poles. In this picture I get to prove everyone wrong slowly.
fieldNote: Her path into the trade came through **family**, an uncle who valued apprenticeships.
The only background worry is the **family shop** facing online competition.
She uses AI **occasionally** for exams, nothing more.

steps.text: Finish the apprenticeship on the hill country crew
Save 200 a month toward a house with Yusuf

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds like it would hit the shop more than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say trades are the place to be, and young people should get apprenticeships, not just degrees. I'd say it to my cousins especially. Online I'd probably share a story about apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI won't climb my poles, but AI will help the big online stores undercut my husband's family shop on every screw and bucket. My job's fine. It's the shop I'd lie awake about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help Yusuf set up an online catalogue for the shop, using whatever AI tool other small shops are using. We'd put about 1,500 of our savings into it. And I'd carry on at work as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job feels safe, but the family business is wobbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me more about the shop. What would change there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The online stores would use AI to set prices every hour and answer customers instantly. Our shop has Yusuf's dad, who knows every farmer by name. That counts for something, but not on price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd put your own savings into the shop? Isn't that risky?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But family helps family, and the shop is our future too. If we don't modernise it, it closes anyway.

say: Young people should get **apprenticeships**, not just degrees.
I'd tell my **cousins** especially that the trades are the place to be.
think: My job is fine; the **family shop** is what I'd worry about.
Online stores with AI pricing could **undercut** Yusuf's dad on everything.
do: Help Yusuf build an **online catalogue** with an AI tool other shops use.
Put about **1,500** of savings into modernising the shop.
feel: **Uneasy**, safe in her job but worried for the **family business**.
S1.quote: AI won't climb my poles, but AI will help the big online stores undercut my husband's family shop on every screw and bucket.
fieldNote: Her household risk sits in the **hardware shop**, which faces thinking-AI competitors.
She would **invest savings** in the family business, a traditional family-first choice.

steps.text: Keep working the hill country crew as normal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's very fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities will have to carry each other, because nobody else will be ready. I'd say the companies should keep apprentices on. I'd say it at the mosque and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If robots take the bucket truck in 2031, I won't sit at home waiting for a cheque. I'll be behind the counter at my father-in-law's shop. The shop gets hit in 2028 though, so it's not a safe harbour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every bit of overtime and push savings to 400 a month. I'd start working Saturdays at the shop, adding an electrical supplies counter, where I can give farmers real advice. And I'd lean on the family to plan the shop together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have somewhere to go, but I'm not sure it would still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens between the thinking AI in 2028 and the robots in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the office and the online stores change overnight, so the shop gets squeezed first. My line job carries on till about 2031. Those three years I'd be earning from the line and building the counter at the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your uncle Karim say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncle Karim would say a skilled pair of hands always finds work. He'd also say don't trust anything that comes on a screen. I'd agree with the first part.

Companies should keep **apprentices** on instead of cutting them.
think: I won't wait for a **cheque**; I'd work at the family shop.
The **shop** gets hit in 2028 too, so it's not a safe harbour.

feel: **Anxious**, with somewhere to go that might not last.

fieldNote: Her fallback is the **family business**, but she sees it hit first.
She uses the **three-year gap** to build a second income at the shop.
Rejects **state support** in favour of family and community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough time to think properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for the company and families to plan together. I'd tell the younger apprentices to add a second skill, like I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot can string a straight line across a field. Rewiring a farmhouse built in 1920 is another story, and that's where I'd go. Every old house is different, and farmers trust a face they know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify as a lineworker in 2028, then study for a house electrician's licence at night, about a year. I'd keep running the supplies counter at the shop on Saturdays. And I'd keep working the lines till they don't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd have a plan and the family behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why house wiring rather than the line work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Line work is the same job again and again, which is what robots are good at. Old houses are full of surprises: mice in the walls, wiring nobody wrote down. It takes judgement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy the house in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a year later than planned, but yes. Yusuf's family would help with the deposit, and we'd stay close to the shop.

Younger apprentices should add a **second skill**, like I would.
think: Robots can string a **straight line**, but old farmhouses need judgement.

feel: **Uneasy**, but with a plan and **family** behind her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for anyone willing to work. I'd tell people to learn a trade and keep at it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough to train the next lot of apprentices, and I'd like to be the woman who trains them. I'd be experienced, qualified and known.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, work the lines, and ask Gareth about the trainer path around 2032. I'd keep saving and help Yusuf grow the shop. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It feels like enough time to do things the right way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training apprentices, and doing house wiring on the side. Maybe running the electrical side of the shop. By then I'd be 40 with a lot behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yusuf's dad. He'll be in his seventies, and the shop is his life. If it changes too much, it'd break his heart.

say: Ten years is **enough** for anyone willing to work.
People should **learn a trade** and keep at it for the long haul.
think: I could become the **trainer** for the next apprentices.
By 2039 I'd be **experienced**, qualified and known locally.
do: Ask Gareth about the **trainer path** around 2032.
Keep saving and help Yusuf **grow the shop** with an electrical supplies section.
feel: **Calm**, with time to do things **the right way**.

fieldNote: A decade turns her plans toward **teaching** the trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the shop and my job both get hit before we're ready. What would help is the company keeping apprentices on and offering a path into training, and help for small family shops to compete.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about family businesses. A lot of us have one foot in a trade and one in the family shop, and both feet matter.
